new_statements.rule_in_words: Yupik-type iambic rhythm: counting from the left, stress falls on the 2nd syllable and alternate syllables thereafter (schwa may bear stress), with iambic lengthening of open stressed vowels; long vowels (heavy syllables) are stressed and reset the count; closed syllables, initial and non-initial, carry inconsistent extra weight that can attract stress to a closed first syllable or retract/suppress an expected stress after a closed syllable. Krauss's 1990 addendum from direct elicitation (one speaker, 1985) restates it as: stress on any heavy syllable (short closed or long); word-level stress on the 2nd syllable if the 1st is not long, plus on the 1st if it is short closed; no alternating stress beyond the 2nd syllable; and a syntactically conditioned penult stress that is not word-level.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Main text: rhythmic alternate-syllable stresses on even-numbered syllables after the 2nd (e.g. aɣyúqiqúvik), often disrupted near closed syllables ('skipping'/retraction). Addendum (verbatim): 'Stress is quite absent on the fourth and eighth syllables, proving the inoperativity of the alternate syllable stress beyond the second syllable' in the speech of the 1985 consultant; no primary/secondary ranking is given in either account.
new_statements.exceptions: Long vowel in the 1st syllable takes stress (kēɣniqáquq); fluctuation qantáɣakun ~ qántaɣakun, mantíɣamun ~ mántiɣamun attributed to closed-initial-syllable weight and possibly to dialect mixture within Naukanski (Pouten-Naukan vs Uelen, sec. 3.4); disyllables show 'fairly even weight on both syllables'; no distinctive pre-long-vowel gemination (unlike CAY); overlength contrast possibly lost. Addendum verbatim: 'there are three types of stress placement: 1) general tendency for stress on any heavy syllable (short closed as well as long); 2) stress sometimes on penult, syntactically determined, not word-level stress; 3) word-level stress on second syllable (if first not long), along with the stress on first if short closed.'
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level prosody inferred philologically from Menovshchikov's (1975) accent marks in texts, paradigms and lexicon plus one tape of connected narrative (Nutetein); Krauss warns the phonetics are 'delicate', affected by unsorted discourse-level factors, and possibly by dialect mixture. The 1990 addendum separates word-level stress (types 1 and 3) from a sentence-level penult stress (type 2), example qiqmíɣaraɣasùxłuraraɣáqa 'my nice poor little doggie'.
new_statements.identity_note: Krauss's 'Naukanski' = Naukan Yupik (nauk1242, East Cape Siberian Yupik), data from Naukan-village speakers recorded by Menovshchikov 1948-1971, an Oslo tape of the narrator Nutetein, and (addendum) speaker Antonina Verbitskaya, Moscow 1985; Krauss suspects internal dialect mixture (Pouten-Naukan vs Uelen varieties). The Menovshchikov 1997 Jazyki mira stress paragraph describes 'Asiatic Eskimo' based mainly on Chaplino (Central Siberian Yupik, cent2128) and must not be used for nauk1242. Glottolog's ref 'Menovshchikov 1980 Jazyk eskimosov Beringova proliva' concerns Big Diomede (Imaklik) Inupiaq, not Naukan.

new_statements.quote: The major point is that N lacks the alternate syllable stress common to all AY and CSY. For example, that Naukanski qìqmíɣarayasùxłurarayáqa 'my nice poor little dog' has no stress on the 4th and 8th syllables (at -ray- and -rar-) proves conclusively the absence of this basic rule (for AV). [p. 2] ... The main specific Naukan prosodic trait at word-level is the stress on second syllable (if the first is not long and therefore stressed, or in words of more than three syllables with closed first syllable and long closed third). This stress might be related to the Yupik alternate syllable stress rule [p. 4]

Parts NY970K1977-04 and -06 are offprint/ts. copies of the published Krauss 1985 paper (same text, not new). Handwritten parts (1985-01 'VOK J…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Krauss's 1985-86 draft, based on Antonina Verbitskaya (AV, Moscow, Dec. 1985): heavy syllables attract prominence -- long vowels take stress with raised or falling pitch (except word-finally) and short closed syllables take a lesser, pitchless prominence (p. 3); apart from that, word-level stress falls on the SECOND syllable unless the first is long (then the first is stressed), with a further exception in words of more than three syllables whose first syllable is closed and whose third is long and closed (p. 4); a phrase-final penultimate high pitch is added at discourse level (p. 2). Stressed open-syllable vowels are little or not at all lengthened, unlike AY and CSY (p. 2). No alternating stress beyond syllable 2 in AV's speech. For the older speakers Nututein and Eqaluk (1950s tape) Krauss adds (p. 5): 'The alternate syllable stress principle is indeed present in their speech (e.g. Nututein sitúxwaaɣumáluku), though not entirely consistently; it appears occasionally to fail. There appears moreover to be some lengthening of the vowel of syllables so stressed when open, though this too is not nearly so consistent or prominent as in CSY.' Krauss 1993 ts. p. 9 sums up: 'not gone into here or yet known in 1985 - the simplification or atrophy of the Yupik prosody (stress and vowel lengthening) in modern Naukanski.'
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not described as secondary stress. Two prominence types besides word stress: closed-syllable prominence (amplitude, no pitch rise) and a phrase-level high pitch on the phrase-final penult ('the second-last, with phrase-final stress (discourse level)', p. 2). In Nututein/Eqaluk's speech alternate syllables carry rhythmic stress sporadically; Woodbury's restatement of Krauss's rules (NY970K1985-02, p. 3, scanned-verified): '1. Mark stress (high or falling pitch) on heavy syllables. 2. Mark stress (amplitude--and I'd say also lengthening of syllable-final C) on closed syllables. 3. Mark stress (hi tone) on peninitial syllables except when syl. 1 heavy, or in words of >3 syl. where syl. 1 is closed and syl. 3 is long. 4. Mark stress (hi tone) tone on penultimate phrasal syllable. 5. For Nututein and Equaluk, stress every second unstressed syllable (after having applied rules 1-4). (Rule is optional and sporadic.)'
new_statements.exceptions: Speaker/dialect variation is the main caveat: pp. 5-6 'Either then there have been for some time (at least) two prosodically different dialects of Naukanski, one with vestigial or incipient prosody, as represented by AV, the other with better preserved or more fully developed Yupik prosody, as represented by N-E; or the differences within Naukanski are more or less generational'. Initial closed-syllable prominence is 'overshadowed' by the following second-syllable stress (p. 3). Woodbury (letter p. 1-6) hears more variability on the Nututein tape than the rules predict: CV.CV words sometimes with no stress on either syllable, occasional expressive initial-syllable stress, CVC.CVC words stressed on syllable 1 or 2, and suggests the alternate-syllable rule may be 'a matter of genre, and not a matter of intra-Naukanski dialectal variation at all'.
new_statements.identity_note: All statements concern Naukanski proper (Naukan/East Cape Siberian Yupik, nauk1242). Krauss distinguishes speakers, not named dialects: AV = Antonina Verbitskaya (younger speaker, elicited in Moscow, Dec. 1985; vestigial/incipient prosody); N-E = Nututein and Eqaluk (older narrators on the 1950s tape, born perhaps 50 years earlier; Yupik alternate-syllable stress present); Menovshchikov 1975 = 1948 texts and lexicon. The NY970K1985 folder also holds Chaplinski (CSY) and Diomede Inupiaq material (phone notes), which is not about Naukanski.

readall_conflicts: Krauss's own sources disagree and he says so: Menovshchikov 1975 and the 1950s Oslo tape (Nututein, Eqaluk) show the Yupik alternate-syllable (deuterotonic) stress perturbed by long vowels and closed syllables (the published 1985 paper and the catalog reading), whereas Antonina Verbitskaya's 1985 speech 'lacks the alternate syllable stress common to all AY and CSY' beyond a second-syllable word stress, with stress otherwise on heavy syllables and a phrase-final penult pitch rise (draft pp. 2-4). Krauss reconciles this as two prosodic dialects or a generational loss/simplification (pp. 5-6; the 1990 addendum calls the second-syllable stress 'probably a vestige' of alternate-syllable stress; the 1993 ts. speaks of 'atrophy of the Yupik prosody.. in modern Naukanski'). Woodbury's 1986 letter proposes instead that alternation may be genre-conditioned and hears more optionality on the tape than Krauss's rules predict. None of this changes the type: stress placement is weight-driven with a default on the second syllable; only the extent of rhythmic alternation is disputed. Dorais 2005 is silent.
